# Shepherd of Hermas Chapter 19 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Translator:** SOPHIA | **Source:** Codex Sinaiticus (ch 1-31) / P.Mich. 130 (ch 32+), Shepherd of Hermas 19 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-EC/SHE_019_page_001.jpg

---

## Vision 3, Chapter 11

**1** He answered me: "Listen and understand. The stones from the plain placed in the building — the square, white ones that fit precisely at the joints — these are the apostles and bishops and teachers and deacons who walked in the holiness of God and served in their offices with purity and reverence. Some have already fallen asleep; others still live. They were always in agreement with one another, lived at peace, and listened to each other. That is why their joints fit so precisely in the tower." **2** "Those dragged from the deep sea and placed in the building — these are those who suffered for the name of the Lord." **3** "Those brought from the mountains are those who are not new in the faith — those found faithful throughout their lives, honored among the people of God." **4** "But those from the first mountain, which was black — these are apostates and traitors of the church, and blasphemers against the Lord in their sins, and those who are ashamed of the Lord's name. These are dead to God; they cannot be placed in the building and are of no use." **5** "Those from the second mountain, which was bare — these are hypocrites and teachers of wickedness who corrupt God's servants, especially those who are sinners. They have no repentance moving upward in them, but blasphemous words remain in their mouths. These are stones — but only barely."

---

### Council Notes

The twelve-mountain interpretation begins here and will continue through ch. 21. Mountains 1 and 2 represent the most severe failures:
- **Mountain 1 (black):** apostates, church-betrayers, blasphemers — "dead to God"
- **Mountain 2 (bare):** hypocrites and teachers of evil who corrupt others

The phrase "dead to God" (v. 4) is a stark formulation — the opposite of "living to God" (zōn tō theō) in Paul. These people have crossed a threshold that the Shepherd considers irreversible.

"Stones — but only barely" (v. 5) is deliberately ambiguous. It may mean they are barely useful for the building (perhaps placed in a less visible position), or it may be ironic — barely stones at all.
